quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Look outside — the delivery driver [park] the truck right in front of our building.
quests.hint: The action is happening as you speak — which tense captures that?
quests.explanation: Actions happening right now use the present continuous: 'am/is/are + verb-ing.' Since the subject is singular, 'is parking' is correct.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Hold on, I [type] a reply to the client right now.
quests.hint: 'I' plus an action in progress needs both the auxiliary and the -ing form.
quests.explanation: Present continuous requires the auxiliary 'am/is/are' along with the -ing verb. With 'I,' the correct auxiliary is 'am,' giving 'am typing.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Careful — the kettle [boil] on the stove behind you.
quests.hint: A singular subject in progress right now needs 'is' plus the -ing form.
quests.explanation: 'The kettle' is singular and the action is happening now, so the correct present continuous form is 'is boiling.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Right now, the interns [organize] the files for tomorrow's audit.
quests.hint: The subject 'interns' is plural — pick the auxiliary that matches, along with -ing.
quests.explanation: Plural subjects take 'are' in the present continuous, so the correct form is 'are organizing.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: What [you look] at on your screen? You seem really focused.
quests.hint: In a question, the auxiliary moves before the subject: 'are + you + verb-ing.'
quests.explanation: Present continuous questions invert the subject and auxiliary: 'are you looking,' not 'you are looking' or 'you look.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She can't come to the phone because she [feed] the baby at the moment.
quests.hint: An action happening right at this moment needs the full present continuous form.
quests.explanation: 'At the moment' signals an action in progress, requiring 'is feeding' — the auxiliary 'is' plus the -ing form.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The technician [repair] the printer late last night after everyone left.
quests.hint: A specific past time phrase like 'last night' tells you which tense to use.
quests.explanation: 'Last night' signals a completed past action, so the simple past 'repaired' is correct, formed by adding '-ed.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We [plan] this trip for almost six months before we finally booked it.
quests.hint: Double the final consonant before adding -ed when a short verb ends in a single stressed vowel + consonant.
quests.explanation: 'Plan' doubles its final consonant before adding '-ed': 'planned.' This follows the standard spelling rule for short verbs ending in a single vowel and consonant.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The chef [try] a new recipe for the weekend menu, and it turned out great.
quests.hint: Verbs ending in a consonant + y change the y to i before adding -ed.
quests.explanation: 'Try' ends in a consonant plus 'y,' so the spelling changes to 'i' before adding '-ed': 'tried,' not 'tryed.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The landlord [paint] the hallway over the weekend while we were away.
quests.hint: Identify the completed past action and add the regular past-tense ending.
quests.explanation: 'Painted' is the correct simple past form, formed by adding '-ed' to the regular verb 'paint.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [double-check] every figure in the report before sending it to the board.
quests.hint: Even compound verbs like 'double-check' take the same regular past-tense ending.
quests.explanation: Compound verbs follow the same rule as their base verb: 'check' becomes 'checked,' so 'double-check' becomes 'double-checked.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The committee [review] every application carefully before the final decision.
quests.hint: This past action was completed before the decision was made — what ending shows that?
quests.explanation: 'Reviewed' is the correct simple past form, showing that the reviewing was completed before the decision.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The board [choose] a new director after months of interviews.
quests.hint: 'Choose' is irregular — it doesn't simply add '-ed.'
quests.explanation: 'Choose' has an irregular past form, 'chose,' rather than the regular '-ed' ending. 'Choosed' is not a standard English word.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I [lose] my train ticket somewhere between the platform and the café.
quests.hint: Think of the irregular past tense of 'lose,' which changes its spelling entirely.
quests.explanation: 'Lose' becomes 'lost' in the simple past — an irregular form that doesn't follow the regular '-ed' pattern.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The company [spend] a huge amount on advertising last quarter.
quests.hint: 'Spend' has an irregular past form that shortens the vowel and changes the ending.
quests.explanation: 'Spend' becomes 'spent' in the simple past, an irregular form; 'spended' is not correct English.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We [drive] all night to reach the coast before sunrise.
quests.hint: 'Drive' changes its vowel entirely in the simple past, rather than adding an ending.
quests.explanation: 'Drive' has the irregular past form 'drove.' Adding '-ed' to form 'drived' is a common but incorrect pattern.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The intern [bring] the wrong documents to the client meeting by mistake.
quests.hint: 'Bring' shares its irregular pattern with 'think' (thought) and 'buy' (bought).
quests.explanation: 'Bring' becomes 'brought' in the simple past — an irregular form, not 'bringed.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She [teach] herself to code using free videos over the summer.
quests.hint: This verb's past form doesn't follow the regular '-ed' pattern at all.
quests.explanation: 'Teach' has the irregular past tense 'taught.' 'Teached' is a common learner mistake, but it is not standard English.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [There is] several empty seats near the back of the theater.
quests.hint: Look at the noun right after — is it singular or plural?
quests.explanation: 'There' agrees with the noun that follows it. Since 'seats' is plural, the sentence needs 'There are,' not 'There is.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [There are] a strange smell coming from the kitchen this morning.
quests.hint: Check the noun right after 'there' to find out if it's singular or plural.
quests.explanation: 'Smell' is singular, so the sentence needs 'There is,' matching the singular noun that follows.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [There are] not enough parking spaces for every resident in this building.
quests.hint: This is a bit trickier: focus on the noncount phrase 'not enough parking' rather than 'spaces.'
quests.explanation: Although 'spaces' appears later, the subject of the sentence is the noncount idea of 'parking,' which is treated as singular: 'There is not enough parking spaces' still needs 'is' because the sentence centers on the singular concept of space, not a plural count.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [There is] too many people waiting outside the box office already.
quests.hint: 'Many' typically signals a plural noun — check what follows it.
quests.explanation: 'People' is plural, and 'too many' reinforces that, so the sentence requires 'There are,' not 'There is.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [There are] hardly any traffic on the highway this early in the morning.
quests.hint: 'Traffic' is a noncount noun — does it behave like a singular or plural subject?
quests.explanation: 'Traffic' is an uncountable noun and is treated as singular, so the sentence needs 'There is,' even though 'hardly any' might suggest a plural feel.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [There is] two separate lines for online orders and in-store pickup.
quests.hint: The number word right after 'there' makes the plural clear.
quests.explanation: 'Two lines' is explicitly plural, so the sentence must use 'There are,' matching the plural subject.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: My little sister already [cans] ride a bike without training wheels.
quests.hint: This modal verb never takes an -s ending, no matter who the subject is.
quests.explanation: Modal verbs such as 'can,' 'will,' and 'must' never add '-s,' even with third-person singular subjects. The correct form is simply 'can.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Sorry, but visitors [cans not] enter the lab without a security badge.
quests.hint: The negative contraction of 'can not' has a specific spelling.
quests.explanation: The standard contraction of 'cannot' is 'can't.' 'Cans not' is not a recognized English form.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [Cans] you forward me the invoice before the end of the day?
quests.hint: In questions, modal verbs stay in their base form and simply move before the subject.
quests.explanation: Modal verbs never take '-s,' even in questions. The correct form is simply 'Can you forward...'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: This old laptop [cans not] handle the newest software updates anymore.
quests.hint: The contracted negative form of 'cannot' follows one specific spelling pattern.
quests.explanation: 'Can't' is the standard contraction of 'cannot.' Forms like 'cans not' don't exist in standard English.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: My grandfather finally [cans] send voice messages on his new phone.
quests.hint: Remember that modal verbs stay the same regardless of the subject.
quests.explanation: Since 'can' is a modal verb, it never changes form for third-person subjects — it stays 'can,' not 'cans.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [Cans] I borrow your charger for just a few minutes?
quests.hint: Questions with modal verbs place the unchanged modal directly before the subject.
quests.explanation: Modal verbs form questions by moving before the subject without changing form, so the correct question is 'Can I borrow...'
